messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Linh Tran was caught in the hurricane two years ago, she had been finishing an evening shift at the public library where she worked as a librarian. By the time she left, the town had already gone eerily quiet. The wind had dropped for a short stretch before the worst of the storm hit, and she still remembers how unnatural that silence felt, as if the whole street had stopped breathing. Then the power failed. In the dark, with no streetlights and no sound except distant structural groaning, she was trapped for hours in a neighbor’s ground-floor apartment with several residents from her block, including an older man she knew from the library. They waited in darkness for rescue as floodwater rose and furniture shifted around them. The man panicked, then became quiet in a way she still cannot forget, and Linh has remained haunted not only by the danger but by the helplessness and grief of being there with people whose faces she knew.

In the months afterward, the things that reached her most sharply were not dramatic reminders but the same conditions that had surrounded her that night. If a room suddenly went completely silent, her body reacted before she had time to think. Waking in the dark had the same effect. At the library, when the building settled into hushed stillness after a children’s program ended or during the last minutes before closing, she would feel herself bracing, scanning the room and the windows as if some new emergency were about to arrive. If patrons came in who had also lived through the hurricane, or if she recognized one of the displaced families from that period, she became intensely alert to where everyone was standing and where the exits were. She had grown used to choosing the chair in staff meetings with the clearest path out and the most protection behind her, and when she entered any room she automatically checked corners, doors, and whatever might signal danger.

Those same moments also carried the storm back into the present without warning. Silence in the stacks, seeing someone connected to that night, or opening her eyes into darkness at 3 a.m. could bring the whole scene back fully formed, as though she were again sitting in black water and waiting for something worse. The memory did not come as a story she deliberately recalled; it forced itself into her mind. What overwhelmed her most when it did was grief—grief for the man from her neighborhood, grief for the people huddled together in that apartment, grief for the part of her life that had felt ordinary before that night. She had begun to dread the memory so much that she also started dreading the circumstances that might set it off, and the range of things that counted as reminders seemed to widen over time.

To manage these moments, Linh tried to make herself go blank. When the memory surged up in the dark or in a sudden pocket of silence, she would deliberately attempt to leave her body, staring fixedly or mentally “checking out” until she could feel less. When she sensed herself getting keyed up, she avoided going out for evening walks and stopped exercising altogether because the bodily arousal felt too close to panic. She also arranged her days to avoid circumstances that resembled the storm night: she kept lamps on throughout the house, resisted staying late at work, and asked her husband to handle anything that meant being outside after dark. At the library she sometimes lingered near busier areas instead of shelving in isolated quiet sections, because the stillness there made her feel too exposed.

But the harder she worked to shut herself down and avoid those conditions, the less control she seemed to have over the memory. Blankness offered only brief relief; the image of the dark apartment would break through anyway, abrupt and unwanted, sometimes after she had spent the whole day trying not to think about it. Avoiding darkness and silence left them feeling even more charged, so that even a brief nighttime awakening or a sudden lull in sound seemed to strike with greater force. Her constant watchfulness fed the same pattern. Because she was always on guard—always checking exits, reading the room, deciding where it would be safest to sit—small shifts in the environment stood out immediately, especially silence, darkness, or the presence of someone tied to the hurricane. Once noticed, they became harder to dismiss, and the memory came faster.

Over the last year this has narrowed her life. She still works, but colleagues have noticed that she resists closing alone and appears tense in quiet corners of the building. Her husband has grown frustrated by how many lights she leaves on and how often she refuses evening plans. Linh finally sought help after waking in the dark last month and instantly feeling the storm all over again, followed the next day by a freeze-like spell at work when the library fell silent and a patron from her old neighborhood approached the desk. What frightens her most is that her mind now seems able to turn almost any darkness or silence into that night, and that she will keep disappearing from her own life in order to get through it. What she hopes, carefully, is not to erase the memory but to stop living as if the storm is always about to begin again.
